claims.text: Controlled Ti addition combined with spark plasma sintering at 1600 °C will produce in situ TiC precipitates in WxTaTiVCr.
The resulting TiC precipitates will be nanoscale and uniformly dispersed.
TiC precipitate interfaces will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
TiC nanoprecipitates will preferentially trap irradiation-induced point defects.
Trapping at TiC precipitates will enhance recombination of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies.
TiC precipitates will provide dispersion strengthening.
Enhanced defect recombination will mitigate radiation-induced swelling.
Enhanced defect recombination will reduce irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
The modified alloy will exhibit approximately 30–40% lower post-irradiation defect-cluster density than the unmodified baseline.
The modified alloy may exhibit an approximately twofold increase in hardness relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy will maintain or improve overall mechanical strength under fusion-relevant irradiation conditions.
The proposed benefits will hold at elevated temperatures and ion fluences typical of plasma-facing fusion components.
Non-uniform or oversized TiC precipitates may negate the proposed radiation-tolerance and mechanical benefits.
